scripts.title: The Stoic drill for being insulted
scripts.pattern_evidence: Insider reveal: 4 videos, median 5.2x their creator's Shorts median (Daily Stoic 7.2x and 5.8x, HealthyGamerGG 4.5x, Mind In Context 3.4x). Topic and two-branch turn reuse Moodius's best reel ("Someone disrespected you today?", 16.5 s avg watch, n=1).
hooks: What a Stoic actually did when someone insulted him.
Someone insulted you today. Here's what Epictetus trained for.
The Stoics had a drill for being insulted.
cards: What a Stoic actually did when someone insulted him.
He didn't hit back. He didn't swallow it either.

THE QUESTION
Is it true, or is it just loud?
If it's true, it's information. If it's false, it's theirs to carry.
Either way, an insult needs your agreement to land.
Send this to someone still replaying today.

scripts.caption:
Not every insult deserves a reply. Some don't even deserve your agreement.

Epictetus taught a simple drill: before you react, ask whether it's true. If it is, you've learned something. If it isn't, it was never about you.

Which one was today's?

Evidence: philosophy (Epictetus, Enchiridion 20), in our words.
scripts.first_comment: True or just loud? One word.
scripts.save_share_reason: A one-question tool they can use tonight on a specific person; 'send this to someone still replaying today' names the person to send it to.

scripts.title: Too sensitive, or well informed?
scripts.pattern_evidence: Question about something you were told as fact: 6 videos, 2 with a usable baseline, median 3.7x (HealthyGamerGG 5.1x, Mind In Context 2.3x). We keep the shape and drop the medical topic: Moodius makes no medical claims.
hooks: Is being "too sensitive" a flaw, or is it information?
Someone once told you that you were too sensitive.
"You're too sensitive." Who benefited from you believing that?
cards: Is being "too sensitive" a flaw, or is it information?
Sensitivity notices things: a tone shift, a lie, a room going cold.
That's not a defect. It's a sensor.

BUT
A sensor isn't a verdict.
Notice the feeling. Then check the facts before you act on it.
"Too sensitive" was never the problem. Unexamined was.
Send this to the person who needed it at fifteen.

scripts.caption:
A lot of us were told we were too sensitive before we had words for what we were noticing.

Sensitivity picks up real signals. The skill isn't feeling less. It's checking the signal before you act on it. Epictetus called it testing the impression.

Who told you, and were they right?

Evidence: philosophy (Epictetus, Enchiridion 1.5), in our words. Reflection: Moodius.
scripts.first_comment: What does your sensitivity usually notice first?
scripts.save_share_reason: Reframes a label many people carry from childhood. The CTA names who to send it to (someone who was called 'too sensitive' young).

scripts.title: Lonely at a full table
scripts.pattern_evidence: Second-person scene: 2 videos at 1.8x and 2.2x their creators' medians, both text over still scenes (the Moodius format). On Moodius, 3 reels with this shape held a median 41% past 3 s vs 32% for the account.
hooks: You were lonely at a full table, and nobody noticed.
Laughing at dinner. Lonely the whole time.
Have you ever been lonely around people who love you?
cards: You were lonely at a full table, and nobody noticed.
Because you were laughing. You're good at laughing.
Loneliness isn't the absence of people...
...it's the absence of being known by them.

TRY THIS
Tell one person one true thing this week.
Not everything. One thing. The table stays full, and gets less lonely.
A Moodius reflection, not a study.
Send this to the one who laughs the loudest.

scripts.caption:
Some of the loneliest evenings happen in company. You're there, you're funny, and nobody actually knows how you are.

You don't fix that by finding more people. You fix it by letting one of them know one true thing.

Who would you tell?

Evidence: Moodius reflection (opinion, not a study).
scripts.first_comment: One true thing you haven't said out loud this month. Only if you want.
scripts.save_share_reason: People share what they can't say. Sending it to 'the one who laughs the loudest' is a way of saying 'I see you'.

scripts.title: The cost of always replying straight away
scripts.pattern_evidence: Hidden cost: 1 video so far, but at 9.5x its creator's median (Human Friction, 'The psychological cost of being available', 1,005 views vs 106). One example is a lead, not proof. This reel tests it.
hooks: You answer every message within a minute. Here's the cost.
Being always available is teaching people something.
The quiet cost of always replying straight away.
cards: You answer every message within a minute. Here's the cost.
Every instant reply teaches people your time is free.
So they stop asking whether it's a good moment.

THE COST
Your attention, cut into pieces nobody asked for.
Seneca noticed we guard our money and hand out our time.
Reply in an hour. That's the whole cost of keeping your evening.
Idea: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 3 · Moodius words
Save this for the next time your phone lights up.

scripts.caption:
Fast replies feel polite. Over time they teach people that your attention is always on tap.

Seneca made the point two thousand years ago: we're careful with money and careless with time. An hour's delay costs the message nothing. It might give you your evening back.

How fast do you usually reply?

Evidence: philosophy (Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 3), in our words.
scripts.first_comment: Honest answer: what's your average reply time?
scripts.save_share_reason: Gives a concrete permission (reply in an hour) people want to keep and point to later; the save CTA ties it to the moment they'll need it.

scripts.title: Rest or avoidance?
scripts.pattern_evidence: X vs Y: 2 videos, 5.4x and 1.5x their creators' medians (HealthyGamerGG 'Depression vs Responsibility'). Built as Moodius's two-branch structure, which held 16.5 s average watch once (n=1). Discipline is reframed as a feeling, per the 22 Oct lessons.
hooks: Rest or avoidance? They feel the same from the sofa.
Is it rest, or are you hiding?
Two people skip the gym tonight. Only one is resting.
cards: Rest or avoidance? They feel the same from the sofa.
Same sofa. Same blanket. Different reason.
Ask one question: what am I moving toward?

IF IT'S REST
You'll get up wanting to do the thing.

IF IT'S AVOIDANCE
You'll get up wanting more sofa.
Rest refills you. Avoidance only postpones you.
Idea: Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind 17 · Moodius words
Save this for the next sofa night.

scripts.sound: 'dawn' ambient bed; two alternating low notes, one under each branch card (4 and 5); bed brightens slightly on card 6
scripts.caption:
Rest and avoidance look identical from the outside. The difference is what you get up wanting.

Seneca was in favour of rest: he wrote that the mind comes back keener after a break. Avoidance doesn't give you that. It just moves the thing to tomorrow.

Which was your last evening?

Evidence: philosophy (Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind 17), in our words.
scripts.first_comment: Rest or avoidance: what was yesterday?
scripts.save_share_reason: A two-branch test they can run on themselves next time; it removes guilt from real rest, which people like to share.
